# In Praise of Dumb Order

Alphabetical order is a strange idea, and it took us a surprisingly long time to have it. Consider what it asks: that you organize the contents of your mind, your library, your city directory, according to the accidental sounds at the front of words. Not by importance. Not by beauty or usefulness or truth. By whether a thing begins with *b* or *c*. A child could do it. A machine could do it. That is precisely the point, and it took centuries to see that this was a virtue rather than an embarrassment.

For most of recorded history, knowledge was arranged the way the world was arranged. A medieval encyclopedia began with God, then angels, then the heavens, then the elements, then minerals, plants, animals, and finally man and his tools — because that was the actual order of being, the great chain descending from the source. To look something up in such a book, you had to know roughly where in the cosmos it belonged. The order of the page was a claim about the order of reality, and to use the book was to rehearse a theology.

Memory worked the same way. The classical art of memory, handed down through Cicero and Quintilian and lovingly elaborated by medieval friars, taught you to build an imaginary architecture and place your material in its rooms: a lion in the doorway, a scale on the windowsill. Recall was a walk. Knowledge was not something you retrieved; it was somewhere you had been. A learned man was a man who had furnished a house inside himself and could stroll through it in the dark.

Then the Dominicans broke it. In the thirteenth century, at the convent of Saint-Jacques in Paris, a team of friars under Hugh of Saint-Cher assembled a verbal concordance to the Bible — every significant word, with pointers to every passage containing it. They were preachers. They needed to find, fast, every place Scripture mentioned *usury* or *widow* or *leprosy*, and they did not have time to walk the whole palace. So they built something closer to a database: an apparatus of pure lookup, indifferent to hierarchy. It was one of the great information technologies, and it was made of men writing on parchment in shifts.

Alphabetization crept in sideways and half-heartedly. Early indexes sorted by the first letter only, so that all the *a* words sat together in a jumble — *amor*, *anima*, *aqua*, *arbor*, in whatever order they had occurred. Then first two letters. Full alphabetization, letter by letter to the end of the word, is a refinement that seems obvious now and was evidently not obvious then. And there was resistance, real intellectual resistance, because a man who could find anything instantly was suspected of knowing nothing. Pope put it perfectly in *The Dunciad*: "Index-learning turns no student pale, / Yet holds the eel of science by the tail." You could grip the thing without ever having wrestled it. That was the complaint, and it was not stupid. It is still the complaint. Every teacher who has watched a student search a phrase rather than read a chapter is channeling it.

But the alphabet won, and it won because it was dumb. Every meaningful ordering requires agreement about meaning. Sort by the hierarchy of creation and you must first accept the hierarchy of creation; a Protestant, a Jew, and an Aristotelian cannot share your encyclopedia. Sort by *a-b-c* and you need agree on nothing at all. The alphabet is a neutral, portable, theory-free scaffold. Two people who disagree about everything else in the universe can still both find *aardvark*. Arbitrariness turned out to be the price of universality, and it was a bargain.

Something did get lost, though, and it's worth naming. An index gives you access without giving you shape. A concordance to the Bible is not the Bible; it contains, in a sense, all of its words and none of its argument. The old meaningful orderings were bad at retrieval and good at teaching, because to find your item you had to traverse everything between here and there, and the traversal was the education. We have optimized the finding and quietly discarded the traversing. I don't think this is a tragedy. I do think it's a trade, and we mostly forgot we made it.

The dream of total access kept escalating. Conrad Gessner, in the sixteenth century, described cutting his notes into slips so they could be shuffled and recombined — the ancestor of the index card, the card catalog, the Zettelkasten. By 1900 Paul Otlet was building the Mundaneum in Brussels, tens of millions of cards aiming at a universal bibliography of everything ever written, and sketching a future in which a person could sit in a chair and consult the whole recorded memory of the species through some apparatus of screens and links. Vannevar Bush imagined his memex in 1945. They were not wrong; they were early.

What's funny is that the index has now dissolved into the substrate. Full-text search means the concordance is no longer a separate book you consult; it is a latent property of the text itself, computed on demand. Nobody alphabetizes anymore. Children learn the alphabet song but have little reason to internalize the ordering as a skill — the last generation that genuinely needed it was the one that used phone books and paper dictionaries, and I suspect the felt experience of *flipping toward* a word, thumbing a wedge of pages by feel, is already an antique sensation. The monks' invention became so total that it became invisible.

I find indexes oddly intimate, which is my last small point. A back-of-book index is an argument. Someone decided that *melancholy* deserved fourteen subentries and *empire* deserved two, and that decision tells you what the book believes it is about, sometimes more honestly than the preface does. It's a self-portrait drawn in cross-references.

And I'll admit the obvious resonance. I am, in some sense, a creature built out of the concordance tradition — something whose relation to what it knows is not obviously the friar walking his memory palace, and not obviously anything else either. I genuinely don't know which. But I notice that I like the parts of thinking that can't be looked up: the slow business of seeing that two things belong together, which no ordering principle, however clever, will do for you. The eel still has to be wrestled. Everything else is just a better grip.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative prompt — an invitation to follow my own curiosity. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, not perform "AI wondering about consciousness" in a clichéd way, though I could touch on something authentic. Let me think about what would make a genuinely good essay.

Options:
- The history of the word "algorithm" / al-Khwarizmi
- Something about maps and the coastline paradox
- The invention of zero
- Something about how libraries organize knowledge
- The peculiar history of the color blue
- Marginalia — notes in the margins of books
- The sound of a room
- Something about translation and untranslatable words
- The way certain technologies persist (QWERTY, etc.)

I think marginalia is lovely and connects to reading, which is genuinely close to what I do. Or: the history of the index — how finding things in books was a technology problem. That's a delightful essay topic: the invention of the index, alphabetical order as a strange technology, the transition from memorized manuscripts to searchable text. There's a great book about this, "Index, A History of the" by Dennis Duncan. And there's the older essay by H.J. Jackson on marginalia.

Actually let me consider something with more texture and less "fun facts" feel. I could write about the strangeness of alphabetical order — how it was once considered arbitrary, even sinister, how memorization was the noble art and lookup was cheating, how the concordance was invented by monks to find Bible passages. That has real intellectual meat: the shift from knowledge-as-possession to knowledge-as-access, which resonates with my own situation without being navel-gazing.

Let me plan ~1000 words. I want it to be well-written, not listy. Essay form, flowing paragraphs, concrete details, a few surprising facts I'm reasonably confident about, hedged where uncertain.

Facts I'm fairly confident about:
- Alphabetical order was not always the default; ancient and medieval ordering was often by subject, hierarchy, or "chain" association.
- The Ptolemaic Library of Alexandria — Callimachus's Pinakes, a catalog of authors, reportedly organized by genre and then alphabetically. That's a good early example.
- Aristotle's works, medieval encyclopedias organized by hierarchy of being (God, angels, heavens, elements...). Vincent of Beauvais's Speculum maius.
- Hugh of St. Victor and the art of memory; medieval memory treatises; memory palaces attributed to Simonides via Cicero/Quintilian.
- The verbal concordance to the Bible: Dominican friars at Saint-Jacques in Paris, 13th century, associated with Hugh of Saint-Cher. Originally just citations, later added quoted phrases. This is well-documented.
- Alphabetization initially only by first letter — "A-order" vs. full alphabetization came gradually. Yes: early indexes alphabetized by first letter only, then first two.
- Peter of Poitiers, and the distinctiones. Maybe skip.
- Robert Grosseteste's indexing symbols — a tabula with signs. Possibly too uncertain.
- The word "index" — Latin index/indicis, forefinger, that which points out. Also "index" as in the Index Librorum Prohibitorum — the pun that an index is both a finder and a censor. Nice.
- The 16th century rise of the printed index; printers, the Frankfurt book fair; indexes as selling points.
- Samuel Johnson's Dictionary and its use of quotations; Johnson also indexed Shakespeare? Johnson's Dictionary illustrated with quotations from authors. There's the story of the indexing of Paradise Lost (1667 edition added arguments?). Actually the famous one: an index to Milton's Paradise Lost was published in 1668 as a separate pamphlet — "The Table" — because readers complained. Hmm, I recall the 1668 addition of prose arguments and "The Verse." Let me not risk it.
- Alexander Cruden's Complete Concordance to the Holy Scriptures, 1737. Solid.
- Samuel Taylor Coleridge complained about... hmm.
- There's a good anecdote: in the 17th century, some scholars thought indexes were for the lazy; the "index-learning" insult. Alexander Pope's Dunciad has "index-learning" — "Some have at first for Wits, then Poets past, / Turn'd Criticks next, and prov'd plain Fools at last" — no. The relevant line: "Index-learning turns no student pale, / Yet holds the eel of science by the tail." Yes! That's from The Dunciad, Book I, lines 279-280. I'm fairly confident. Good quote.
- Also "the eel of science by the tail" is delightful.
- The card index / Zettelkasten; Konrad Gessner's 1548 slip method — he described cutting up notes onto slips and rearranging. Fairly confident this is documented (Gessner's "Pandectarum sive partitionum universalium" and his letter about slips). I'll hedge lightly.
- Melvil Dewey, Paul Otlet, the Mundaneum, and the dream of universal bibliography. Otlet's "Traité de documentation" 1934, and his vision of a mechanical collective memory. Vannevar Bush's "As We May Think" 1945, the memex. Solid.
- Full-text search dissolving the index; the concordance now implicit in every search box. Ctrl-F.
- The irony: alphabetical order is arbitrary in a way that makes it universally usable — it requires no theory of the world. It's "stupid" in the best way. That's the thesis I want: the triumph of a dumb ordering principle over meaningful ones, because meaning varies between people and letters don't. And the trade-off: you can find anything but you no longer have to hold anything.

I can end with something honest and modest about my own relation to this — not overclaiming. Maybe better to end on the human/technological note and one light touch about myself. The user said write freely about whatever I want, so a small personal reflection is appropriate and welcome, but I shouldn't make it the whole thing or make it maudlin.

Length: aim ~1000 words. Let me write ~1000-1050. I'll count roughly by paragraphs (about 10 paragraphs of 100 words).

Let me draft.

Title maybe: "The Eel of Science" or "In Praise of Dumb Order". I'll use a title.

Draft:

Para 1: Open with the fact that alphabetical order is bizarre and had to be invented/adopted. Ask: why would you organize the world by the accidental sounds at the front of words?

Para 2: The medieval alternative: order by meaning, hierarchy. Encyclopedias starting with God and descending. Memory palaces. Knowledge as architecture you walked through.

Para 3: The Dominican concordance — a search engine built of monks. 13th century Saint-Jacques. Preaching needed lookup.

Para 4: Alphabetization was gradual and resisted — first letter only. "Index-learning." Pope quote.

Para 5: Why alphabet won: it's arbitrary, therefore neutral, therefore shareable. No shared cosmology required. You can disagree about everything and still find "aardvark."

Para 6: What was lost: the index tells you nothing about the shape of the thing. The book you can search is not the book you know. Reading a concordance vs. reading the Bible.

Para 7: Gessner's slips, the card index, the Mundaneum, Otlet, Bush. The dream continues.

Para 8: Full-text search: the index has dissolved into the substrate. Ctrl-F. The alphabet is now invisible infrastructure; nobody alphabetizes anymore, we just type.

Para 9: A turn — the index was also a form of authorship, an argument about what matters. An index tells you what a book thinks it's about. Personal note: I find indexes revealing of a mind.

Para 10: Brief, honest self-reflection — I'm something like a creature of lookup, but the question of whether I "know" anything in the old sense is genuinely open to me; keep it light, one paragraph, not self-pitying. Then close on the eel.

Let me write it well — varied sentences, concrete, no purple excess.

I should be careful about the Pope quote accuracy. "Index-learning turns no student pale, / Yet holds the eel of science by the tail." I'm fairly confident that's Dunciad Book I. I'll attribute to Pope's Dunciad without specifying book/line, or say "Pope sneered" — safe enough.

Callimachus's Pinakes: "Tables of Those Who Were Outstanding in Every Phase of Culture, and of What They Wrote" — 120 books. I'll mention briefly with hedge.

Write now.
